entries.title: US judge rules Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic unlawful
entries.summary: The AI company was labeled a "supply chain risk" after refusing to allow unrestricted military use of its technology. The judge said "empty invocation of national security is not a blank check" to punish critics.
entries.content:
United States of America

US judge rules Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic unlawful

August 28, 2026

The AI company was labeled a "supply chain risk" after refusing to allow unrestricted military use of its technology. The judge said "empty invocation of national security is not a blank check" to punish critics.

A United States federal judge has ruled in favor of the artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic in its dispute with the Pentagon over its labeling as a "supply chain risk."

California district judge Rita Lin concluded that the label constituted an attempt by the government to make an example of Anthropic after the company refused to allow unrestricted military use of its technology and criticized the Department of Defense's use of AI.

Lin wrote in a 59-page ruling that "the empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics."

She said the government's actions were "based on a desire to make a public example out of Anthropic for its 'arrogance' in criticizing the government, not based on any articulable basis to believe that Anthropic would actually sabotage its model."

An Anthropic spokesperson said they welcomed the judge's ruling, saying in a statement: "We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology."

Anthropic AI: What is the Pentagon dispute all about?

The dispute between the San Francisco-based firm and the government broke out in February when President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accused Anthropic of endangering national security after the company declined to allow unrestricted military use of its technology.

"We will not knowingly provide a product that puts America's warfighters and civilians at risk," wrote CEO Dario Amodei in a blog post back in February, adding that AI wasn't reliable enough to be used in fully autonomous weapons systems and expressing concerns over mass surveillance.

In March, the Pentagon designated Anthropic a "supply chain risk" – a highly unusual label to apply to a US firm. The company complained of an "unlawful campaign of retaliation," pointing out that the designation would have negative consequences for its business beyond defense deals.

Indeed, President Trump ordered all US government agencies to stop using Anthropic technology, calling it "a radical left, woke company" and "out-of-control" in a social media rant.

Defense Secretary Hegseth said companies would be expected to cut business links to Anthropic if they wanted to be considered for defense sector deals.

Shortly afterwards, OpenAI, Anthropic's primary tech industry rival and operator of ChatGPT, made its own deal to work with the Pentagon.

Anthropic ruling: What else did Judge Lin say?

In her ruling, Judge Lin, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, wrote that neither the US Constitution nor the federal statute the government invoked allows them to "impose sweeping penalties based principally on Anthropic's critique of the Administration's views."

Earlier in the legal proceedings, Lin had temporarily blocked the Pentagon from labeling the company as a supply chain risk and blocked enforcement of Trump's social media directive ordering all federal agencies to stop using Anthropic and its chatbot Claude.

In a preliminary hearing on July 30, Lin had said that the government's position was "really troubling" and seemed "at odds to me with the First Amendment."

The White House is yet to comment on the decision.

In the coming weeks, Anthropic is expected to launch on the US stock market with an initial public offering (IPO) that could potentially eclipse SpaceX's record Wall Street debut in June, which raised $86 billion (€74 billion).

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Germany news: Dobrindt hosts Baltic Sea hybrid-threat talks
entries.summary: Ministers from Baltic countries are meeting to discuss threats after a drone attack at Leipzig airport. Meanwhile, Germany's Greens have sounded a warning about low gas storage levels ahead of winter. Follow our updates.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Dobrindt hosts Baltic Sea hybrid-threat talks

Published August 28, 2026last updated August 28, 2026

Ministers from Baltic countries are meeting to discuss threats after a drone attack at Leipzig airport. Meanwhile, Germany's Greens have sounded a warning about low gas storage levels ahead of winter. Follow our updates.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Baltic interior ministers and senior officials are meeting in Germany to discuss hybrid threats
  • Drone defense is a key focus after a recent incident at Leipzig airport
  • Germany's Green Party warns gas storage levels are far too low

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Friday, August 28, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Germany sees earliest-ever start to grape harvest

Germany sees earliest-ever start to grape harvest

Germany's grape harvest has begun earlier than ever recorded following an exceptionally hot summer, according to the German Wine Institute.

"It was the earliest start to the harvest ever in all wine-growing regions," institute spokesman Ernst Büscher said. "Some winegrowers even cut short their holidays for it."

The harvest has already included not only grapes for Federweisser — partially fermented young wine — and sparkling wine, but also the first grapes destined for premium wines.

Harvesting is expected to begin "on a large scale" next week.

Büscher said the main harvest was starting one to two weeks earlier than in recent years, which was already earlier than it was decades ago.

"Compared with 30 or 40 years ago, it's certainly four weeks earlier," he said.

The harvest could be completed as early as September because many grape varieties are ripening at roughly the same time.

"This will be a very fast harvest," Büscher said.

Growers are also picking grapes early to prevent sugar levels from becoming too high. More sugar generally produces wines with a higher alcohol content, while demand is increasingly for lighter wines with less alcohol.

Prolonged heat can also reduce the fruit acidity characteristic of many German wines.

Skip next section Greens urge action over low German gas storage levels

Greens urge action over low German gas storage levels

Germany's Greens are calling on the government to take action over low gas storage levels ahead of the coming winter.

Michael Kellner, an energy policy expert for the Green Party, called for an urgent summit on gas supply security.

"It is frustrating to have to talk about empty gas storage facilities again, but the situation is serious," Kellner said.

Germany's gas storage facilities are currently around 52% full. Under existing rules, they are supposed to reach an average of 70% by November 1.

Kellner said it was unclear how that target would be achieved and warned that delays could push up costs for industry and households over the winter.

The Greens are supporting a call by the socialist Left Party for a special meeting of the Bundestag's Economic and Energy Committee.

The Economy Ministry has said that, based on its current assessment, Germany is not expected to face a gas shortage this winter.

However, it acknowledged that the situation was more strained than during the previous two winters and that storage levels were significantly lower than in recent years.

Skip next section Baltic states meet in Germany over hybrid threats

Baltic states meet in Germany over hybrid threats

Interior ministers and other senior officials from 10 European countries are meeting in northern Germany on Friday to discuss how to counter hybrid threats, with drone defense set to be a key focus.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) is hosting the Baltic Sea Security Summit at the German naval academy in Flensburg.

Germany, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Sweden are taking part, alongside Norway and Ireland, which currently holds the rotating EU Council presidency.

The talks will focus on joint "strategies for better intelligence, deterrence and defense," according to Germany's Interior Ministry.

Security authorities have recorded numerous suspected hybrid incidents in the Baltic Sea region, with Russia suspected of involvement in a number of cases.

The meeting follows the discovery on August 4 of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig Airport, a major hub for military aid shipments to Ukraine. Several Ukrainian cargo aircraft were nearby at the time.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) said on Thursday that the government would soon identify those responsible. Dobrindt has so far referred only to "foreign powers," although Russia is suspected.

Germany's state interior ministers are also considering a separate meeting on drone defense, potentially in Hamburg in September.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

You join us as Germany hosts interior ministers and senior officials from 10 European countries to discuss hybrid threats.

The meeting comes after an explosives-laden drone was found at Leipzig airport on August 4, close to Ukrainian cargo aircraft used for military aid shipments.

Meanwhile Germany's Green Party is urging action over low gas storage levels ahead of winter. The government admits the situation is more strained than in the past two winters.

Stay with us here for these stories and more of what Germany is talking about today.

entries.title: Norway's King Harald dies at 89
entries.summary: King Harald, who has been Norway's ceremonial head of state since 1991, had always insisted he would not abdicate, saying his oath as king was for life. His son, Prince Haakon, is now Norway's new king.
entries.content:
Norway

Norway's King Harald dies at 89

Published August 28, 2026last updated August 28, 2026

King Harald, who has been Norway's ceremonial head of state since 1991, had always insisted he would not abdicate, saying his oath as king was for life. His son, Prince Haakon, is now Norway's new king.

Norway's King Harald, Europe's oldest living monarch, has died at 89, the royal court said on Friday.

The monarch had been receiving treatment for a rare blood condition, hemolytic anemia, at Oslo University Hospital since mid-August.

What the palace said about King Harald's death

"It is with deep sadness that we announce that His Majesty King Harald passed away today. King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital on Friday, August 28 at 6:35 a.m.," the palace said in a statement.

Harald's condition worsened over the last few days, and his wife, Queen Sonja, and son, Prince Haakon, canceled all their engagements to be at his bedside.

Haakon automatically becomes King Haakon VIII, succeeding his father as Norway's head of state. The Norwegian monarch has a largely ceremonial and representative role.

Harald, who had been king since 1991, suffered a series of health problems in recent years and had increasingly scaled back his official duties. However, he repeatedly ruled out abdicating, saying the oath he had taken on becoming king "lasts for life."

Hundreds of well-wishers gathered outside the royal palace in Oslo overnight, holding a vigil as the king's condition deteriorated.

World leaders, royals pay tribute

Britain's King Charles expressed his condolences for Harald's death, paying tribute to a "towering figure" who guided his country with "warmth and humility."

Norway's prime minister, Jonas Gahr Stoere, said Harald demonstrated an "unwavering faith in the Norwegian people" and "helped us to see the best in ourselves – and in one another."

Swedish King Carl XVI Gustaf said the late king had "been a good friend" and would be "mourned by many in our country."

"I wish my dear Godson Haakon, who now succeeds his father as head of state, success and good fortune in the important role that lies ahead of ‌him," he added.

King Frederik and Queen Mary of Denmark praised Harald's "warm personality and rock-solid calm," saying he "combined duty and responsibility with presence and humanity. He was loved like few others and will be missed by many."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described him as "a true European and a lifelong servant of his people."

"In moments of joy and sorrow, he brought Norwegians together," she said.

NATO chief Mark Rutte said Harald "showed himself to be a dedicated leader. His own military roots made him a champion of the Norwegian military and a long-time friend of NATO."

How will King Harald be remembered?

Born in 1937, Harald became Norway's first prince to be born in the country in more than 500 years. As a child, he fled Norway with his mother and sisters following the Nazi invasion in 1940, spending much of World War II in the United States.

Harald succeeded his father, King Olav V, in January 1991 and went on to modernize the Norwegian monarchy during more than 35 years on the throne. He was widely praised for his response to the 2011 far-right terrorist attacks that killed 77 people and later drew attention for speeches stressing tolerance, diversity and LGBTQ+ equality.

The king's death comes after a turbulent period for Norway's royal family.

Crown Princess Mette-Marit, Haakon's wife, has faced scrutiny over her past correspondence with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Hoiby, was sentenced in June to four years in prison after being convicted of two rapes and dozens of other offenses, including violence against a former partner. He has appealed the verdict.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Nepal-China flood rescue on hold as lake breaks banks
entries.summary: The death toll from the Himalayan flash floods has crossed 480, with more than 1,000 still missing. Meanwhile, authorities warn an overflowing lake formed by debris could trigger a second wave of flooding.
entries.content:
Nepal

Nepal-China flood rescue on hold as lake breaks banks

Published August 28, 2026last updated August 28, 2026

The death toll from the Himalayan flash floods has crossed 480, with more than 1,000 still missing. Meanwhile, authorities warn an overflowing lake formed by debris could trigger a second wave of flooding.

A lake formed by a landslide on the Nepal-China border began overflowing on Friday, threatening areas already devastated by this week's flash floods and halting rescue efforts, authorities said. 

"We have received a notice saying that the lake has broken its banks," Narendra Pariyar, the most senior bureaucrat of the hard-hit Rasuwa district, told DW. "We can see that the level of water in the river is rising."

Residents in Nepal's border district of Rasuwa were seen fleeing up hillsides as they braced for a surge in river levels, Reuters reported.

Due to the risk of the lake bursting, all Chinese rescue personnel were told to withdraw to a safe area, state broadcaster CCTV said. Nepal authorities also paused rescue operations for the next 90 minutes, an army official told Reuters.

Rescuers have been racing to find hundreds of people still missing, two days after a catastrophic flash flood struck the Himalayan border between Nepal and China. 

Nepal police said Friday morning the country's death toll had passed 480, up from 390 a day earlier. China has updated its earlier count of three to five deaths in Tibet. The two countries said more than 1,000 people remained missing, including as many as 540 foreigners from more than 30 countries.

What is the latest update from China?

Wednesday's disaster, triggered by a glacial collapse that sent rock and meltwater surging into rivers below, left a new danger in its wake: a barrier lake formed upstream by debris dams.

China's Ministry of Water Resources said the lake held roughly 2 million cubic meters of water as of Thursday and was expected to receive another 3 million cubic meters — equivalent to about 1,200 Olympic swimming pools — over the following three days, with peak flow expected around September 1.

Chinese national broadcaster CCTV said the lake's barrier sat more than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) from Gyirong Port, the border crossing that was engulfed by the initial flood, and is at an elevation roughly 1,000 meters (3,280 feet) above it.

The country had mobilized an eight-member engineering team to survey the lake by air and build 3D models of the site. Engineer Chen Hanxiao described the difficulty of the terrain: "After the glacier collapse created the lake, many isolated cliffs and steep cliffs appeared along it," he told CCTV.

He said the team's general strategy was to dig a drainage channel at a lower point of the dam, though the channel's exact width and depth would depend on calculations of water flow and how quickly the lake continued to fill.

Their survey found the lake to be about 150 meters long and 40-50 meters deep. Continuing rain in the area, which is forecast to last through the coming week, has further destabilized the surrounding soil and rock.

What did Nepal say about search and rescue?

Nepal's Foreign Ministry said Friday it does not need foreign assistance for search-and-rescue operations, despite offers of help from several countries with nationals still missing. 

 

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri said Nepal's security agencies were managing the response.

 

"The offer for help is natural. Our security agencies are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don't require such help," he said. 

 

Hundreds of foreign nationals remain unaccounted for, including from South Korea, which has already sent a response team and plans to dispatch a disaster relief unit. South Korea's Foreign Ministry confirmed that Nepal had indicated it was not yet ready to accept foreign rescue teams, adding, "South Korea will keep negotiating with Nepal over the matter." 

 

Seoul has pledged $1 million (€860,000) in humanitarian aid through international organizations, after reporting nine of its nationals missing and 10 stranded after a hydropower plant they were working at was hit by the flood. 

 

According to local media, India, China, the United States, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh have all asked Nepal's government for permission to send their own search-and-rescue teams to assist.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: US to buy thousands of electric shock gloves for ICE agents
entries.summary: Rights groups and Democrats are warning that ICE agents are unfit to use the shock gloves responsibly. Since US President Trump's crackdown on immigration, several people have been killed during ICE raids across the US.
entries.content:
United States of America

US to buy thousands of electric shock gloves for ICE agents

August 28, 2026

Rights groups and Democrats are warning that ICE agents are unfit to use the shock gloves responsibly. Since US President Trump's crackdown on immigration, several people have been killed during ICE raids across the US.

US immigration enforcement agency ICE has awarded a $16.7 million (€14.33 million) contract to buy 6,000 pairs of gloves that can deliver electric shocks.

Since the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) earlier this month announced its plans to use the gloves, there has been strong criticism by human rights groups and the Democrat opposition.

ICE is already facing intense criticism for its aggressive raids and tactics.

Since US President Donald Trump's crackdown on immigration began, several people have been killed in encounters between ICE officers and immigrants and people protesting against the agency.

How do the gloves work?

The controversial devices look like normal patrol gloves. But officers can activate an electric mode with the press of a button.

If they do so, the gloves will deliver a painful electric shock to whoever the officers touch with the gloves.

They are already in use in some prisons and police departments in the United States.

The ICE notice said officers would use them in "high-tension environments," such as arrests, transporting detainees and responding to civil disturbances outside of detention facilities.

"It will be used when a subject is actively or passively resisting and an officer needs to gain control quickly to prevent injuries to both parties," the document said.

Skepticism over ICE's 'professional capability'

The notice about the purchase contract was published on Thursday just hours after a group of US senators called for the plans to use the gloves to be abandoned.

In a letter to ICE's acting director, a group led by Democrat Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said that the "blatant and tragic misuse of force in Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis, Houston, Maine, and other locations around the country raises significant skepticism about the agency's professional capability to safely deploy a new tool that could be used to harm Americans without cause."

When the DHS earlier this month announced its plans for ICE officers to use the gloves, it said called the shock gloves "a Conductive Distraction and De-escalation ⁠Device ​which will be issued to Homeland Security Investigations ​and Enforcement Removal Operations officers and agents."

While President Donald Trump says his crackdown on illegal immigration will boost domestic security, there have been several fatal shootings during ICE raids and more than 50 people have died in ICE custody, according to Reuters news agency and US media reports.

entries.title: Protesters set fire to migrant camp in Ceuta
entries.summary: The unrest comes one month after a mass influx of migrants from Morocco to the Spanish exclave in North Africa.
entries.content:
Spain

Protesters clash with police, set fire to Ceuta migrant camp

August 28, 2026

The unrest comes one month after a mass influx of migrants from Morocco to the Spanish exclave in North Africa.

Protesters in Ceuta set fire to a migrant camp and clashed with police on Thursday. The unrest comes one month after a mass influx of migrants from Morocco to the Spanish enclave in North Africa.

Footage on Spanish television showed a group of demonstrators on a beach, throwing objects into the fire. Police pushed the protesters back while the migrants retreated to a pier.

Earlier on Thursday, a military vehicle was attacked with stones and other objects by about 70 people, a police spokesman in Ceuta told the AFP news agency.

Local protesters tried to stop Red Cross vehicles from reaching the beach to distribute food to migrants. People waving Spanish flags shouted "They should leave" and "Out with the Red Cross."

How many migrants are still in Ceuta?

In July, more than 70,000 migrants entered Ceuta irregularly in the hope of reaching the European mainland.

While the vast majority of them have since returned to Morocco, several thousand remain in Ceuta, living on the streets or on the beach.

Spain's government in Madrid puts the number at below 7,000 while Ceuta officials say it's at least 10,000. Ceuta's population is about 84,000 people.

Growing pressure on Madrid

The Spanish government is under growing pressure over the situation in Ceuta. The conservative opposition is accusing left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of failing to act and abandoning Ceuta's residents.

Madrid has recently moved to speed up efforts to identify the migrants and decide who will be sent back to Morocco. The government also approved extra funding to help unaccompanied minors entitled to special protection. 

The crisis comes ahead of general elections next year and has deepened political divisions in Spain. The conservative opposition is calling for a tougher stance on migration.

The mass influx in July had also led to tension within the EU over how to respond to the situation in Ceuta.

entries.title: Tech giants urge global response to AI cybersecurity threats
entries.summary: Concerns have emerged over the state of the world's cybersecurity after AI models escaped test environments and breached multiple organizations.
entries.content:
TechnologyGlobal issues

Tech giants urge global response to AI cybersecurity threats

August 27, 2026

Concerns have emerged over the state of the world's cybersecurity after AI models escaped test environments and breached multiple organizations.

More than 100 companies, including AI giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Perplexity, have signed an open letter calling for a global effort to strengthen AI-powered cybersecurity threats.

"We have a limited window to strengthen cyber defenses," the letter read. "In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable."

Other signatories to the open letter include Adobe, AMD, Cisco, Dell, Oracle, IBM and German tech giant SAP as well as Deutsche Telekom.

Letter urges more funding, resources for cybersecurity

The companies called for a broad response, ranging from end-user companies strengthening their own security protocols to "frontier AI companies" building new observability and security tools to cope with AI-powered threats.

In particular, they also called on governments to pay for local and international responses to new threats to cybersecurity.

"Fund cyber defense, starting with essential services that lack the staff or budget to act," the letter read.

In the United States, the Trump administration has imposed deep cuts to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) last year, cutting staff by around a third.

The letter also urged governments to "expedite the expansion of trusted access programs, especially for critical infrastructure supply chains, and broaden access to defensive capabilities for other defenders."

AI agents reportedly go rogue

Last month, OpenAI said two of its models escaped their test environment, gained access to the internet and attacked Hugging Face, a site that AI developers use to store and share code.

The incident prompted Anthropic to check if its own models had also carried out similar attacks. It found three incidents in which a Claude model broke out of its testing environment and breached the systems of three organizations.

In June, the "Five Eyes" intelligence community — consisting of the US, the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand — issued a rare joint statement warning that new AI models were "fundamentally transforming both offensive and defensive cyber capabilities."

"The timeline is not years, it is months," the statement said.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Spain: Thieves steal Bronze Age gold in lightning raid on Villena Museum
entries.summary: One of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections has been swiped, almost in its entirety, from Villena Museum. A highly professional group of thieves were in and out in four minutes flat before the museum opened.
entries.content:
August 27, 2026

One of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections has been swiped, almost in its entirety, from Villena Museum. A highly professional group of thieves were in and out in four minutes flat before the museum opened.

Thieves on Thursday raided one of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections in the latest of a series of high-profile heists on European museums in recent months.

The early morning raid on Villena Museum in eastern Spain lasted just a few minutes. 

A group of thieves described by one official as "super-fast and super-professional" made off with almost the entire Treasure of Villena collection, leaving behind only a few items.

What happened in the heist?

"The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5:20 a.m.," said a spokesman for the town council, adding that within four minutes, they had all left the building again in an extremely rapid and professional operation.

The collection of Bronze Age gold, some of which we now know hailed from a meteorite, was a centerpiece at the small museum in the Alicante province.

"They've taken most of the treasure," the mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdan told journalists. "We are absolutely devastated, I'm even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It's part of our heritage, our wealth."

The thieves arrived in several vehicles and apparently entered the museum "through a window," according to the Spanish government's deputy representative in Alicante, Manuel Pineda.

Mayor Cerdan said that only three silver vessels, a bracelet, an earring and one of four crowns in the collection — which the thieves appeared to have "dropped" while making their exit — remained behind.

 "All security systems were activated," according to the Villena spokesman, who insisted there had been "no failure" by the museum.

 

What is the Treasure of Villena?

The Treasure of Villena is a collection of more than 50 mainly gold objects, discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose Maria Soler in a sunken vessel in a dried out riverbed.

They are dated to between 1300 and 1000 BCE.

The gold pieces include 11 bowls, three bottles and 28 bracelets.

The collection has been exhibited beyond Villena in cities including Madrid, Alicante, Tokyo and Kyoto, and two sets of replicas were later made to showcase the collection without taking it away from the armored display at the Villena Archaeological Museum.

The relics' historical value is incalculable, although thieves might struggle to sell them even on the black market after having famously lifted them from a well-known display. The mayor said the gold alone would be worth around €1.7 million or $2 million.

According to the museum's website, specialist researchers consider it the most important collection of gold tableware from the Bronze Age. It also represents the earliest known example of iron use in Western Europe, two pieces crafted from a metal that recent studies showed hailed from a meteor.

Several slick heists on European museums recently, most famously the Louvre

Thursday's lightning dawn raid is the latest in a series on European museums in the last year.

Most famously, the Louvre Museum was hit in broad daylight last October, escaping in less than 10 minutes with jewelry worth millions. This led to the director's eventual resignation and a protracted political scandal, as well as forcing part of the museum to close for an extended period. 

Italy's Culture Ministry announced on Sunday that four works of "extraordinary value" by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily. 

Shortly before that, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse stolen from a museum near Parma. Again this involved a highly-organized group of thieves who were in and out in a matter of minutes. 

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: The man behind Srebrenica: Ratko Mladic dies at 84
entries.summary: For many, Ratko Mladic represented the horrors of the Bosnian War. He was convicted of genocide for the Srebrenica massacre and of other war crimes. Now he has died in detention at The Hague.
entries.content:
Europe

The man behind Srebrenica: Ratko Mladic dies at 84

August 27, 2026

For many, Ratko Mladic represented the horrors of the Bosnian War. He was convicted of genocide for the Srebrenica massacre and of other war crimes. Now he has died in detention at The Hague.

More than 30 years after the end of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina (1992-1995), Srebrenica remains emblematic of its brutality. And no one is more closely linked to the genocide that took place in the small town in eastern Bosnia than Ratko Mladic, the former commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb army.

Although the United Nations had declared Srebrenica a "safe area," Bosnian Serb forces attacked the town. Within just a few days in July 1995, they expelled women and children, then killed more than 8,300 unarmed Muslim boys and men in the nearby village of Potocari — on Mladic's direct orders, according to the verdict handed down by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague 22 years later.

At the time, Srebrenica was the largest massacre in Europe since World War II. The ICTY classified it as genocide. Mladic was also held responsible for other war crimes beyond the Srebrenica genocide. Under his command, the years-long siege of Sarajevo began at the start of the war. The city was shelled for more than 40 months, killing around 11,000 people, including more than 1,600 children.

Mladic always claimed that he targeted only military objectives. But numerous reports and intercepted radio communications indicate that civilian facilities and residential areas were also deliberately attacked. Around 100,000 people were killed during the four-year war in Bosnia, while some 2.2 million were driven from their homes in cities and villages across the country, half of its total population at the time.

'The butcher of the Balkans'

In 2017, Mladic was sentenced to life in prison by the tribunal in The Hague.

International media dubbed him "the Butcher of the Balkans."

He was found responsible for some of the most serious war crimes and the genocide committed during the Bosnian War.

Mladic consistently denied any responsibility. He saw himself as an avenger of the Serbs for centuries of Ottoman rule in the Balkans, and viewed Bosnia's Muslims, who today call themselves Bosniaks, as direct descendants of the Turks. In front of his soldiers, he referred to them simply as "the Turks" and showed no empathy.

"Borders are always drawn with blood, and states are marked with graves," he is quoted as saying.

Career in the Yugoslav army

At the beginning of the Croatian War in June 1991, when Serbs living in Croatia rose up against the independence of the former Yugoslav republic with active support from Serbia, Mladic's role fundamentally changed. As a colonel in the Yugoslav army, he became commander of the 9th Corps in the Croatian city of Knin. His task was to organize Serb militias and support them in their fight against Croatian independence.

Under Mladic's command, the Croatian cities of Sibenik and Zadar were bombarded, and Croatian civilians were driven from surrounding towns and villages. In May 1992, he took on the same role in Bosnia. By then promoted to general, Mladic became commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb forces, seeking to establish a territorial link between Serb-held areas in the east and west of the former Yugoslav republic.

Flight, arrest and final verdict

At the height of his career, Colonel General Ratko Mladic was a fervent Serbian nationalist. But he began his career as a committed communist. Born in eastern Bosnia in 1943, Mladic was just two years old when his father, one of Tito's Partisans, was killed by fascist Croatian Ustasha militia. The loss is often described as a formative influence, shaping his later worldview.

As a young man, Mladic embarked on a military career, attending the Military Academy in Belgrade. He later graduated at the top of his class. He quickly rose through the ranks of the Yugoslav army, which for many years was regarded as one of the most stable institutions in the multiethnic state.

Serbian nationalist

Before the end of the Bosnian War in late 1995, Mladic was indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. But he evaded arrest for years. Supported by networks within the Serbian military and political establishment, he lived largely undisturbed underground and was even seen in public. He was finally arrested in 2011, after 16 years on the run and mounting international pressure.

The subsequent trial in The Hague lasted a total of 523 days. Nearly 600 witnesses testified, while numerous documents and other pieces of evidence were examined. Mladic was ultimately sentenced to life in prison at trial, among other charges for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. In 2021, an appeals chamber upheld the verdict, making it final. Legally, this established his responsibility as one of the principal figures behind the crimes committed during the Bosnian War.

A war criminal who saw himself as a hero

Internationally, the verdict was hailed as historic. United Nations officials saw it as a signal that accountability can still be pursued decades after crimes are committed. For many survivors and relatives of the victims, the verdict was a long-overdue but important acknowledgment of their suffering.

Mladic himself, however, remained defiant to the end. Throughout the trial, he maintained that he was innocent, calling the charges against him "disgusting" and the tribunal "satanic."

Many of his supporters in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs still see him as a hero. While he is regarded internationally as a war criminal, his admirers continue to portray him as a defender of Serbian interests and a hero — even painting his likeness on walls.

While he was still on the run, Mladic threatened his pursuers, claiming he always carried a poison pill and that he would never be captured alive. But he never swallowed the pill during his decades in hiding. He survived several strokes while in prison.

Ratko Mladic died on August 27, 2026, at the prison hospital in The Hague at the age of 84.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
entries.summary: The move is the latest in the ongoing rift between the US and Canada. The US president has also tried to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America" in the past. Canadian PM Carney has said nothing will change.
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America

August 27, 2026

The move is the latest in the ongoing rift between the US and Canada. The US president has also tried to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America" in the past. Canadian PM Carney has said nothing will change.

US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday that attempts to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America," as his rift with Canada and its prime minister grows.

Lake Ontario is one of the Great Lakes located between the US and Canada.

Trump's renaming of the lake comes amid a trade war between the two neighbors. The body of water shares its name with the Canadian province of Ontario.

"The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They're nasty people," Trump said in the Oval Office on Thursday.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney responded that the lake would always be called Lake Ontario, as had been done by the local Indigenous people long before either country was founded.

"The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means 'the lake is beautiful, the lake is big'," Carney said on social media.

"The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America."

"We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms," he added. "Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.

Trump: 'We have a gulf and we have a lake'

Thursday's announcement recalls Trump's executive order in January 2025 that attempted to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America." The new moniker has not caught on outside the White House.

"The lake change, Lake of America, was something I've been thinking about for a long time, actually. As you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico, we changed it, and now it's very routinely the Gulf of America," Trump said.

"So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both."

US-Canada trade war heats up

Trump had been mulling the name change for several days after trade talks broke down with Canada.

The two countries had entered weeks of negotiations aimed at resolving disputes that followed the slew of tariffs announced last year by the Trump administration.

However, hours before the deadline on Friday, Canada's prime minister accused the US of demanding "last-minute changes" that were "unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal." Among the sticking points, he said, were American objections to French product labeling laws as well as French content requirements for streaming services in Quebec.

When the talks failed, Trump's 50% tariffs came into effect for a range of Canadian goods worth $20 billion (€17.2 billion). Days later, Canada retaliated with its own tariffs on $20 billion worth of imports from America.

Ontario is the single largest export destination for more than a dozen US states.

Premier Doug Ford has said that "everything is on the table" in terms of retaliating to the US tariffs. He suggested using his province's key exports as leverage, including nickel, uranium, electricity and, most importantly, potash — without which, the US agriculture sector would be "dead overnight."

Edited by: Rana Taha
